items.title: Sinan Brought Water to Istanbul but Died in a House Without It
items.moral: Moral: Do not place excessive trust in fame, worldly privilege, or human remembrance. True service is rendered not for personal gain, but for what one knows to be right.
body: During the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, Istanbul was growing rapidly and faced a severe water shortage. The task of solving it fell to the great architect Koca Sinan (1489–1588).
One day, the sultan summoned him and asked:
“Chief architect, people pay dearly even for a packhorse’s load of water. Can Istanbul be supplied with enough water?”

Sinan requested permission to survey the surrounding country. With his assistants, he examined wells, valleys, and streams from Çekmece to Beşiktaş and calculated where dams and aqueducts could be built.
When he returned, he told the sultan:
“It can be done, but at a heavy price: sacks filled with gold would have to be placed end to end.”
The sultan replied:
“Tell me only that it is possible. If necessary, I will place the sacks not end to end, but side by side.”
Sinan began work and created a magnificent system culminating in forty public fountains across the city. Taps were fitted so that the precious water would not be wasted.

The sultan declared the public fountains the property of the people and prohibited secret pipes into private homes. In recognition of Sinan’s service, however, he verbally allowed a private line to the architect’s house.

Years passed. Suleiman and those who had witnessed Sinan’s service died. One day, the elderly architect was summoned to the palace, where the council was investigating a complaint about the private water supply to his home.
Sinan explained that the sultan himself had granted permission. When asked for a written decree, he admitted:
“At the time, I was ashamed to ask the Ruler of the World for a document. I have no written order.”
After a long debate, the council decided not to punish Sinan for his past use of the water, but ordered the private line cut off.
Near the end of his life, Sinan fell gravely ill. When those beside him tried to moisten his lips, the tap was dry. The great architect said:
“We did not serve for profit, but for Allah’s pleasure. We await our reward in the hereafter and do not grieve that this world has denied water to our home.”

items.title: Life After Sixty
items.moral: Moral: After years of caring for others, allow yourself to enjoy life too. Your happiness can brighten the lives of those around you.
body: It is time to use the money you have saved up so far. Use it and enjoy it. Don’t save it for those who know nothing of the sacrifices you made to earn it. This is the ideal time to enjoy peace.

Do not worry about the financial situation of your children and grandchildren, and do not be upset that you have spent your money on yourself. You have taken care of them for years, taught them everything you could. You have given them education, food, shelter and support. Now it is their duty to earn their own money. Let them find their own way.
Take care of your health without overexerting yourself. Exercise moderately, walk each day, eat well, and get enough sleep.

At this age, it is easy to get sick and difficult to stay healthy. Therefore, you should keep yourself in good shape, pay attention to your medical and physical needs. Contact your doctor; get check-ups even if you feel fine.

Do not let small troubles consume you. You have already faced much in life and carry both happy and painful memories. Do not let the past hold you back or the future frighten you. Enjoy the present; many everyday worries will soon be forgotten.
Whatever your age, keep loving your partner, your family, and life itself. A lively mind and a compassionate heart can keep you young in spirit.

Keep caring for your appearance and well-being. Visit the hairdresser, care for your nails and skin, and look after your teeth. Feeling well groomed can lift your spirits and strengthen your confidence.

Don't lose sight of age-appropriate fashion trends, but maintain your own style. Read books, flip through newspapers, watch the news. Go online, find out what people think. Make sure you have an active email account and use at least a few social networks.
Respect younger people and their opinions. They may disagree with you, but they must find their own way. Offer advice rather than criticism, and share the wisdom of your experience.
Never use the phrase "in our time...". Now is your time. Be a part of this time as long as you live.
Spend less time with people who leave you feeling discouraged and more with those whose company brings you joy.
Do not give up your hobbies. You can travel, walk, cook, read, dance. If you want, you can keep a cat or a dog.

Get out of the house, meet people you have not seen for a long time, and either experience something new or relive something from the past. The main thing is to get out of the house from time to time. Go to museums, walk in the park.
Try to always be polite, do not complain and criticize unless necessary. If someone has broken your heart, forgive them. Apologize to those whose hearts you have broken.

Don't carry your pain with you. It will only hurt you. It doesn't matter who is right. They say that holding a grudge is like poisoning yourself and waiting for someone else to die. Never accept that poison. Forgive, forget and move on with your life.
Laugh, enjoy yourself, and welcome the peace this stage of life can offer.

items.title: A Wise Father’s Advice to His Son
items.moral: Moral: Wisdom is the source of happiness, and strength is the servant of wisdom. He who listens to advice will be exalted; but he who thinks he knows everything will perish.
body: My beloved son,
Cultivate the understanding that helps you build good relationships. It is an inexhaustible source of happiness and joy.
Our desire for life is never fully satisfied. Whether a life is long or short does not determine its worth.
Fruit is ready to fall only when it is ripe. In the same way, people have always valued the wisdom that comes with experience.
In youth, people often do wrong without thinking. Later, the memory of those wrongs can pierce the heart like a dagger.
Those who follow an honest path in youth earn respect in old age.
Strength is a good thing, but it must be guided by reason.
Allah, the Creator of all worlds, did not place us here to live forever. Every life must come to an end.
Through many trials, Allah has taught me two habits that have helped preserve my health: eating modestly and walking after meals.
I also want you to understand that there are three kinds of people.
The first think clearly and can look ahead to the consequences of their actions.
The second lose their way through the influence of others, but are willing to listen when someone offers guidance.
The third know little, yet believe they know everything and refuse all advice. They are the most unfortunate of all.
My son,
If you belong to the first group, I will be glad.
If you belong to the second, listen to good advice.
Do not become one of the third. Such people earn favor neither with Allah nor with others.

items.title: The Goose to Be Plucked
items.moral: Moral: A wise word is revealed to those who understand it. Not everyone understands what they hear — some answers a person must find for themselves.
body: On a bitter winter day, a king went out in disguise with his chief vizier. Beside a stream they met an old tanner dipping hides into the icy water and beating them.
The king greeted the old man:
“Peace be upon you, venerable elder.”
“And upon you, ruler of the world,” the old man replied.
“What did you do during the six?” the king asked.
“Unless you add six to six, you cannot feed thirty-two,” the tanner replied.
The king asked again:
“Did you never rise in the night?”
“We did, Your Majesty, but others benefited.”
The king laughed and asked his last question:
“If I send you a goose, will you pluck it?”
“Certainly—and without making it cry out.”
The king and vizier walked on. The king asked:
“Did you understand our conversation?”
“No, Your Majesty,” the vizier admitted.
The king grew angry.
“Find out what it meant by this evening, or you will lose your head.”
After escorting the king home, the frightened vizier hurried back to the stream. The tanner was still at work.
“What were you and the king talking about?” he asked.
The old man looked him up and down.
“I don’t give answers for nothing. Pay me a hundred gold coins.”
The vizier handed over the coins.
“How did you recognize the king?”
“I’m a tanner. No one else could afford the fur he was wearing.”
The vizier scratched his head.
“What did you mean about adding six to six to feed thirty-two?”
The tanner collected another hundred coins before answering.
“He asked why I hadn’t earned enough during the six warm months to rest in winter. I told him I had to work all twelve months to feed the thirty-two teeth in my mouth.”
The vizier went on:
“And what did he mean about rising in the night?”
The tanner accepted another hundred coins.
“He was asking whether I had children to support me. I told him I had daughters, but they had married and now belonged to other households.”
The vizier lowered his head.
“And the goose he said he would send?”
The tanner laughed.
“That one you can work out for yourself.”

items.title: Hayat’s Life Story
items.moral: Moral: Blind custom and a false idea of “honor” can destroy a woman’s life, a child’s life. Those who look away from early marriage, violence, and neglect are partners in that oppression.
body: When my mother left our home, my father, and us, I was six and my brother was eight. Even at that age I understood why she left my father, but I could not understand why she left us. Would a mother abandon her children?
My father used to beat my mother. He beat me and my brother too. I came to believe that all men beat their wives and children…

After my mother left, home became four walls. No one called us to wash our faces because breakfast was ready. No one even asked whether we were hungry, though we might go days without food. The hardest lesson was this: without the comfort of a mother’s presence, a child can grow up overnight. I grew up at six.

About ten days after my mother left, the police came to our house. They said she had taken her own life. In her hand she had been clutching an envelope. On it was written: “To be given to my daughter and my son.”
I could not read then — how was I supposed to read it? My brother read it. I cried as I listened. My brother cried too.

My mother had gone to her father’s house, but he flew into a rage. In his eyes, a woman had to stay with her husband. Even with a mouth full of blood, she was expected to say, “I’ve been drinking red sherbet.” My mother begged him: “Let me stay for a month. Then I’ll find a way to take my children and start again.”

But a woman living alone? To my grandfather, that would disgrace the family. He would never be able to hold his head up again; he said he would rather see his daughter dead. That evening, my mother took her own life. My grandmother told me this years later, on her deathbed, when I was nineteen.

When my father heard of my mother’s death, he was not upset at all. He said he would put us in an orphanage. From then on we would live there; that would be our home. Brother and sister might be parted, forget each other, and years later fail to know each other — so we were both to keep Mother’s letter.

But before I could ask how the two of us would keep one letter, my brother cut it in half with scissors. He gave me the beginnings of the sentences. Since I had the openings, once I learned to read I would have to guess the rest. My brother had already memorized the letter anyway.

When my aunt heard we were to be sent to an orphanage, she came. She told my father: “A girl is not given to an orphanage. I will take Hayat and raise her myself.” Living with my aunt, I understood why: a girl meant an unpaid servant ordered about the house. Not once did my aunt call me by my name. My name became “Come-here”: “Come-here, fetch water… Come-here, wash these dishes…”

Once a month my brother visited me at my aunt’s. He said he was fine in the orphanage. I said I was fine too — I did not want to upset him. Did he also say “I’m fine” so I would not worry? I never dared ask.

I had started school. I was the first in the class to learn to read. How could I not — I was going to read my mother’s letter. The part I still had began: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I…” Every night in bed I tried to finish that sentence:
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I love you so much.”
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I miss you terribly.”
“Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I am waiting for you.”
I built a different dream around each ending. In those dreams, I was happy. Who chooses to dream of sorrow?
I finished middle school. My aunt said I would not go to school anymore. But I wanted to study — to stand on my own feet and live under one roof with my brother.

That summer the wife of Uncle Hasan, the neighbourhood grocer with three children, died of cancer. I was heartbroken. What would the three children do — how would they find a mother’s scent? Why did mothers die? Would those three forget their names as I had, and become “Come-here” too?

While I was grieving for Uncle Hasan’s children, it came out that I was betrothed to him. It turned out I had been sold for eight bracelets and three thousand liras. Because I was too young for a civil marriage, forty days later our religious marriage was performed.

I was fifteen. I was Uncle Hasan’s wife. I had three children — two, five, and six. And my aunt insisted we must have a child of our own… I was supposed to have a child so my place would be secure and Uncle Hasan would not look at other women.

The first slap from Uncle Hasan came because I called him “Uncle Hasan.” Does a woman call her husband “uncle”? When I lost my mother at six, I learned to keep silent. So I did not ask, “Does a man call a fifteen-year-old girl his wife?” — I stayed quiet.

When Uncle Hasan hit me, all three children clung to their father’s legs: “Don’t hit Sister Hayat — she plays with us, she tells us stories,” they begged. I was those children’s older sister. What I called stories were my dreams.

When Uncle Hasan went out, I practiced saying “Hasan” in front of the mirror. But every time I said it, I pictured his thinning hair, his glasses slipping down his nose, and his large belly. Calling him by his name made me feel ashamed, as though I were doing something wrong. One day, his six-year-old son heard me. “Sister Hayat, Mother used to call him ‘Bey,’” he said. “You could call him that too.”

“Bey” — of course, “Bey” would be better. I bent and kissed dark-eyed Sami, who listened to my dreams as if they were fairy tales. I called five-year-old Elif and two-year-old Zahra and began to tell them a story. That day I began: “Once upon a time there was a six-year-old girl named Nagil. Nagil had lost her mother. She searched everywhere; when she could not find her, she went to the land of dreams. There Nagil was so happy that she never returned to the real world.”
In my tale Nagil was always happy, always smiling. Every day I told the children that story. We were very happy.

Uncle Hasan was good too. I now called him “Bey.” From time to time he grew angry, but I understood why: instead of a woman he had bought, for eight bracelets and three thousand liras, a storytelling sister.

My brother came to visit. Each time he wanted to give me his half of Mother’s letter. I would not take it. I was afraid that if I read the other half, I would fall from the land of dreams into a cruel real world and be unhappy. All my dreams were built on that other half.

By the time I was forty, the children who had listened to my stories were grown. Sami had become a doctor and moved to another city. Whenever he felt low, he called and said, “Sister Hayat, tell me a story.”
Elif had become a teacher and married. I had a granddaughter. They badly wanted to name her Hayat; I would not allow it. Elif said, “Then let her name be Nagil.” So my granddaughter’s name was Nagil.
My youngest, Zahra, became a veterinarian. “Sister Hayat, whenever an animal is restless I tell it a story, and it calms down,” she would say. Zahra married too, and I had a grandson.
When I was forty-five, Uncle Hasan—my Bey—died. I grieved for him. His last words were a plea for forgiveness, and I forgave him with all my heart. I remembered the good in him.
But there are others I cannot forgive:
against those who see no wrong in marrying off fifteen-year-old girls, and those who support them;
those who call a daughter’s wish to escape daily beatings a disgrace, and those who stand behind them;
against those who show no mercy to children left helpless and hopeless like wounded birds, and those who support them —
These people I cannot forgive.

TITLE: Hayat’s Life Story
BODY[1]: When my mother left our home, my father, and us, I was six and my brother was eight. Even at that age I understood why she left my father, but I could not understand why she left us. Would a mother abandon her children?
BODY[2]: My father used to beat my mother. He beat me and my brother too. I came to believe that all men beat their wives and children…
BODY[3]: After my mother left, home became four walls. No one called us to wash our faces because breakfast was ready. No one even asked whether we were hungry, though we might go days without food. The hardest lesson was this: without the comfort of a mother’s presence, a child can grow up overnight. I grew up at six.
BODY[4]: About ten days after my mother left, the police came to our house. They said she had taken her own life. In her hand she had been clutching an envelope. On it was written: “To be given to my daughter and my son.”
BODY[5]: I could not read then — how was I supposed to read it? My brother read it. I cried as I listened. My brother cried too.
BODY[6]: My mother had gone to her father’s house, but he flew into a rage. In his eyes, a woman had to stay with her husband. Even with a mouth full of blood, she was expected to say, “I’ve been drinking red sherbet.” My mother begged him: “Let me stay for a month. Then I’ll find a way to take my children and start again.”
BODY[7]: But a woman living alone? To my grandfather, that would disgrace the family. He would never be able to hold his head up again; he said he would rather see his daughter dead. That evening, my mother took her own life. My grandmother told me this years later, on her deathbed, when I was nineteen.
BODY[8]: When my father heard of my mother’s death, he was not upset at all. He said he would put us in an orphanage. From then on we would live there; that would be our home. Brother and sister might be parted, forget each other, and years later fail to know each other — so we were both to keep Mother’s letter.
BODY[9]: But before I could ask how the two of us would keep one letter, my brother cut it in half with scissors. He gave me the beginnings of the sentences. Since I had the openings, once I learned to read I would have to guess the rest. My brother had already memorized the letter anyway.
BODY[10]: When my aunt heard we were to be sent to an orphanage, she came. She told my father: “A girl is not given to an orphanage. I will take Hayat and raise her myself.” Living with my aunt, I understood why: a girl meant an unpaid servant ordered about the house. Not once did my aunt call me by my name. My name became “Come-here”: “Come-here, fetch water… Come-here, wash these dishes…”
BODY[11]: Once a month my brother visited me at my aunt’s. He said he was fine in the orphanage. I said I was fine too — I did not want to upset him. Did he also say “I’m fine” so I would not worry? I never dared ask.
BODY[12]: I had started school. I was the first in the class to learn to read. How could I not — I was going to read my mother’s letter. The part I still had began: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I…” Every night in bed I tried to finish that sentence:
BODY[13]: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I love you so much.”
BODY[14]: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I miss you terribly.”
BODY[15]: “Hayat, my beautiful daughter, I am waiting for you.”
BODY[16]: I built a different dream around each ending. In those dreams, I was happy. Who chooses to dream of sorrow?
BODY[17]: I finished middle school. My aunt said I would not go to school anymore. But I wanted to study — to stand on my own feet and live under one roof with my brother.
BODY[18]: That summer the wife of Uncle Hasan, the neighbourhood grocer with three children, died of cancer. I was heartbroken. What would the three children do — how would they find a mother’s scent? Why did mothers die? Would those three forget their names as I had, and become “Come-here” too?
BODY[19]: While I was grieving for Uncle Hasan’s children, it came out that I was betrothed to him. It turned out I had been sold for eight bracelets and three thousand liras. Because I was too young for a civil marriage, forty days later our religious marriage was performed.
BODY[20]: I was fifteen. I was Uncle Hasan’s wife. I had three children — two, five, and six. And my aunt insisted we must have a child of our own… I was supposed to have a child so my place would be secure and Uncle Hasan would not look at other women.
BODY[21]: The first slap from Uncle Hasan came because I called him “Uncle Hasan.” Does a woman call her husband “uncle”? When I lost my mother at six, I learned to keep silent. So I did not ask, “Does a man call a fifteen-year-old girl his wife?” — I stayed quiet.
BODY[22]: When Uncle Hasan hit me, all three children clung to their father’s legs: “Don’t hit Sister Hayat — she plays with us, she tells us stories,” they begged. I was those children’s older sister. What I called stories were my dreams.
BODY[23]: When Uncle Hasan went out, I practiced saying “Hasan” in front of the mirror. But every time I said it, I pictured his thinning hair, his glasses slipping down his nose, and his large belly. Calling him by his name made me feel ashamed, as though I were doing something wrong. One day, his six-year-old son heard me. “Sister Hayat, Mother used to call him ‘Bey,’” he said. “You could call him that too.”
BODY[24]: “Bey” — of course, “Bey” would be better. I bent and kissed dark-eyed Sami, who listened to my dreams as if they were fairy tales. I called five-year-old Elif and two-year-old Zahra and began to tell them a story. That day I began: “Once upon a time there was a six-year-old girl named Nagil. Nagil had lost her mother. She searched everywhere; when she could not find her, she went to the land of dreams. There Nagil was so happy that she never returned to the real world.”
BODY[25]: In my tale Nagil was always happy, always smiling. Every day I told the children that story. We were very happy.
BODY[26]: Uncle Hasan was good too. I now called him “Bey.” From time to time he grew angry, but I understood why: instead of a woman he had bought, for eight bracelets and three thousand liras, a storytelling sister.
BODY[27]: My brother came to visit. Each time he wanted to give me his half of Mother’s letter. I would not take it. I was afraid that if I read the other half, I would fall from the land of dreams into a cruel real world and be unhappy. All my dreams were built on that other half.
BODY[28]: By the time I was forty, the children who had listened to my stories were grown. Sami had become a doctor and moved to another city. Whenever he felt low, he called and said, “Sister Hayat, tell me a story.”
BODY[29]: Elif had become a teacher and married. I had a granddaughter. They badly wanted to name her Hayat; I would not allow it. Elif said, “Then let her name be Nagil.” So my granddaughter’s name was Nagil.
BODY[30]: My youngest, Zahra, became a veterinarian. “Sister Hayat, whenever an animal is restless I tell it a story, and it calms down,” she would say. Zahra married too, and I had a grandson.
BODY[31]: When I was forty-five, Uncle Hasan—my Bey—died. I grieved for him. His last words were a plea for forgiveness, and I forgave him with all my heart. I remembered the good in him.
BODY[32]: But there are others I cannot forgive:
BODY[33]: against those who see no wrong in marrying off fifteen-year-old girls, and those who support them;
BODY[34]: those who call a daughter’s wish to escape daily beatings a disgrace, and those who stand behind them;
BODY[35]: against those who show no mercy to children left helpless and hopeless like wounded birds, and those who support them —
BODY[36]: These people I cannot forgive.
MORAL: Moral: Blind custom and a false idea of “honor” can destroy a woman’s life, a child’s life. Those who look away from early marriage, violence, and neglect are partners in that oppression.

items.title: Fresh Bread
items.moral: Moral: A child’s sincere prayer and a few generous hearts can transform a family’s day. Where people are willing to share, no one need go hungry.
body: The smell of hot, fresh bread spread throughout the street.
The old man approached the baker. He needed to buy hot bread for his grandson. The child had been asking for fresh bread for days.
People were standing in line to buy bread. He took his place in line.
There weren't many people, and his turn came quickly.
He took the change from his pocket. If he had had enough, he would have bought two loaves. But when he held out the coins, the baker waved them away and handed him a bag.
“Take these, uncle, and enjoy them.”
There were three loaves of bread in the package.
“But I only asked for one loaf.”
“Take all three. You can save some for later.”
The grandfather slowly approached the baker and whispered in his ear:
“I only have enough money for one,” he whispered.
The baker smiled:
“Please take them, uncle. It’s Friday, and every Friday we give away three fresh loaves. Enjoy them.”
“May Allah be pleased with you, my son.”
“Amen.”
He had just left the bakery when someone called out to the grandfather:
“Uncle, wait!”
The grandfather turned and looked:
“Yes, my son?”
“This is my mother’s zakat. We would be grateful if you accepted it.”
The young man put an envelope in the old man's pocket.
“May Allah accept her charity and bless her.”
As he passed the market, a woman called to him:
“Uncle, please wait a moment.”
The old man stopped and looked in the direction from which the voice came. A young woman handed him two full bags:
“We’re sharing food this Ramadan, uncle. Please accept these bags. We’d be so glad if you took them.”
“May Allah accept your kindness, my daughter.”
“Amen.”
The old man reached home with difficulty, exhausted.
“Welcome home, Father.”
“Where’s your mother?”
“In the kitchen. She’s making kaygana, the egg dish Orkhan loves.”
“Take these bags to her, please. My back is aching.”
“Grandpa, did you get fresh bread?” his grandson asked.
“Yes, plenty.”
“Hooray for Grandpa!”
“But Dad, this morning you didn’t even have money for tea.”
“Allah provided, my daughter.”
His wife entered the room:
“Where did all this come from?”
“It’s a gift for us,” he said.
The man told what had happened one by one.
When the call to prayer sounded, they broke their fast with kaygana and fresh bread. The bags also held butter and cheese, which they enjoyed with tea.
“Thank Allah for this meal. May He accept their kindness. The halva is delicious too.”
After eating, his grandson stood up.
“I’m going to my room to pray again.”
“Isn’t it early? You can pray before bed,” his grandfather said.
“I prayed at this time yesterday for warm bread and cheese, and look what came! Now I’ll ask Allah to send money for your teeth. It hurts you to chew.”
His mother smiled:
“I wish your father were here to see this.”
“He visits me in my dreams every night. He told me to pray.”
The old man suddenly remembered his jacket. He went to the hanger, put his hand in his pocket and took out the envelope. There was a large amount of money in the envelope.
His eyes filled with tears.
“What is it? Why are you crying?”
“The Lord has sent everything our grandson wished for. Look—there’s enough here for both of us to have our teeth fixed before the holiday. Praise be to Allah!”

items.title: A Meaningless Question
items.moral: Moral: An answer to a meaningless question cannot lead to truth. A well-formed question is already half the answer.
body: One day, a graduate of the University of California, Berkeley, visited a rabbi in New York and asked for help studying the Talmud.
“Do you know Aramaic? No? What about Hebrew? Were you at least taught the Torah as a child?”
The young man answered no to every question.
“But I defended a dissertation on Socratic logic! I would like to study the Talmud to fill some gaps in my education.”

“The Talmud is one of the greatest works of human thought, but you are not yet ready to study it. Still, since you insist, I will give you a logic question. If you answer correctly, I will teach you. Two people climb down the same chimney. One emerges with a clean face and the other with a face covered in soot. Which one will go and wash?”
“You call that a logic question?” the Berkeley graduate asked confidently. “The person with the dirty face, of course!”

“Wrong. The person with the clean face will see the other’s sooty face, assume that his own face is dirty too, and go to wash. The person covered in soot will see a clean face in front of him and suppose that he has remained clean.”
“A very clever answer! Could you give me another chance?”
“All right. Two people climb down the same chimney. One has a dirty face and the other a clean one. Which will go and wash?”
“But we have just discussed that. The person with the clean face will go.”

“Wrong again. Both will wash. The person with the clean face will see his companion’s dirty face and think that he is dirty too. The other will notice that his companion looked at him and then went to wash, so he will realize that his own face must also be dirty.”
“I hadn’t thought of that. May I try once more?”
“Very well. I will ask for the last time: two people climb down the same chimney. One has a clean face and the other a dirty one. Which will go and wash?”
“Now it is clear: both of them will go!”

“No. Neither will go. The person with the dirty face will see a clean face before him and assume that he is clean as well. The person with the clean face will notice that his companion is not going to wash and conclude that there is no need to do so.”
Growing desperate, the young man begged the rabbi for one more question. The rabbi began:
“Two people climb down the same chimney. One has a dirty face and the other a clean one…”
“Neither of them will wash!” the young man answered hastily.

“Wrong again,” the rabbi said calmly. “You studied Socratic logic. Ask yourself: how could two people climb down the same chimney together and only one get soot on his face? The question itself makes no sense. Spend your life answering meaningless questions, and neither the answers nor the search will give you meaning.”

items.title: Mother and Son
items.moral: Moral: The child who once feared being left may one day leave a parent with the same fear. Caring for parents means attending to their need for love as well as their physical needs.
body: The man set the suitcases against the wall, straightened up, and took a deep breath. “It’s a lovely place, Mom.”
“Of course it is, son,” she replied. For a while they stood silently, looking around the room.
Then the woman opened her small suitcase and took out her nightgown, slippers, a few towels, and a framed picture. She placed the picture on the table next to her bed.
In the photograph, a small boy in school uniform stood stiffly, his eyes brimming with tears and his lips pressed together.

The man approached the window and opened the curtain. A pale daylight filled the room. It was freezing outside. He leaned his hands on the heater and watched the muddy cars passing by for a while. Then, without even turning his head, he asked, “Is this closet enough for you, Mom?”
She did not hear him. Seated on the bed, she was gazing at the frightened boy in the worn frame.
It was a picture they had taken on the first day of school.

The memory returned. The day before school began, she had spent hours telling him how wonderful it would be. Even so, she had barely persuaded him to enter the classroom. She waited all day, reassuring him at every break: “I’m here, son. I’m waiting for you.” He clung to her hand. “Don’t leave me, Mom. I’m scared.”
The sun was setting. Her son moved his warm hands from the radiator to the cold window. “Shall we open the other suitcase and put your things away?”

“Don’t let me keep you. I can do it. There isn’t much.” She reached for his hand with trembling fingers. For a moment she seemed about to say more. Then she swallowed. “The children will be wondering where you are.”
The door closed. She was alone with the peeling paint and the photograph. After a while, she put on her slippers and went to the window. Below, her son was getting into his car.
The old woman was afraid. Despite the fact that she had listened for hours the day before to how beautiful this place was, she was still afraid.
His handprint still marked the glass. She pressed her cheek against it, her eyes filling and her lips trembling.
“Don't leave me, son, I'm so scared,” she whispered.
Her words seemed to melt into the misted glass and flow toward her son as he waved from the car.
That night, the other residents heard her crying. Sobs in the corridor were a familiar sound at the nursing home.

items.title: A Mother’s Love
items.moral: Moral: A mother’s love is unconditional and irreplaceable. Make time for those you love today, because time is the most precious thing we can never recover.
body: Erich Fromm
I am one year old—completely happy, because my mother is always beside me.
I am two—my mother is with me only sometimes. I wonder what is happening.
I am three—my mother is at work, and my nanny is with me.
I am five—my mother is in a meeting, and my grandmother is with me.
I am seven—my mother is at a seminar; I am at school with my teacher.
I am thirteen—a teenager. My mother still has to work, and my friends are beside me.
I am seventeen—my mother comes home exhausted. I am at school, in class, or at a café with friends.
I am twenty—young and confident. My mother is not at home, but my friends are with me.
I am twenty-three—I have started working. My mother is home now, while I am at work.
I am thirty—and I wonder: when did my mother and I last spend real time together? Something is wrong.
I am thirty-five—married. My mother lives in her home, and I in mine.
I am forty—my mother waits for me just as I once waited for her as a child.

Love your child today. Hold them, take their hand, and remain beside them. Do not miss today’s episode, because tomorrow a new scene of childhood will already have begun.

items.title: The Price of a Miracle
items.moral: Moral: Faith is a powerful force. Sometimes, when a child’s pure faith meets the kindness of a human being, a miracle is born.
body: (A True Story)

Lisa was eight years old when she heard her parents talking about her younger brother, Oliver. All the little girl knew was that her brother was very sick and that her parents had no money for his treatment.
Only a very expensive operation could save Oliver. There was no one to lend them money. Lisa heard her father whisper helplessly to her tearful mother, “Only a miracle can save him now.”

The girl went into her room and took out a glass jar that she had kept in a secret place in the closet. She poured out all the money in the jar on the floor and counted it carefully—she did this several times. When she was finished counting, she carefully put the coins in the jar, closed the lid, and went out the back door to the pharmacy.

At the pharmacy, she waited for the pharmacist to notice her. He was deep in conversation and ignored her attempts to attract his attention. Finally, she placed a few coins firmly on the glass counter. He turned, startled.
“What do you need, little girl? I’m talking to my brother. I haven’t seen him in a long time.”
“I need to talk about my brother too,” Lisa said urgently. “He’s ill, and I need a miracle to make him better.”
“A miracle?”
“His name is Oliver. There’s something bad growing in his brain. My parents say only a miracle can save him now. How much does one cost?”
“I’m sorry, but we don’t sell miracles here,” the pharmacist said more gently.
“I have money. If it isn’t enough, I’ll find more. Please just tell me the price.”
A smartly dressed man who had been watching the conversation from the sidelines until now—the pharmacist’s brother—leaned down and asked Lisa:
“What sort of miracle does your brother need?”
“I don’t know. He’s very sick and needs an operation. My parents can’t pay, so I brought my own money.”
“How much do you have?”
“One dollar and eleven cents. That’s all, but I can try to get more.”
“One dollar and eleven cents,” he said with a smile. “What a coincidence. That’s exactly the price of the miracle your brother needs.”
The man took the money from the girl, took her hand, and said:
“Take me home with you. I’d like to meet your brother and your parents. Let’s see what I can do.”
This handsome man was Dr. Carlton Armstrong, a renowned neurosurgeon.
He performed the operation without charge, and Oliver soon came home. His parents were overjoyed. “It’s a miracle,” his mother whispered. “I wonder what that operation would have cost.”
Lisa smiled. She knew the price: one dollar and eleven cents, and a little girl’s faith that her brother could be helped.

items.title: Parenting
items.moral: Moral: A child is educated not with fear, but with love. It is not a teacher or an outsider who educates a child—it is a loving parent.
body: A boy constantly defied his parents, neglected his schoolwork, and refused to do his homework. His mother’s blows and his father’s punishments changed nothing.
One day, on the way to school, his mother saw a crowd around a bear trainer. As the man beat a tambourine, a bear with a ring through its nose performed for the spectators.
“I can’t manage my own child,” she thought, “yet this man can train a bear.”
She approached him. “How do you make that wild animal obey? I can’t get my son to listen.”
“Everything has its method,” he said with a smile. “I have mine.”
“Then please help me.”
The trainer looked at the boy. “Bring him to me for a week. I’ll make him obedient.”
The woman was happy and started taking the boy to the bear trainer every day.
Within days, the boy became quiet and compliant. By the end of the week, his mother was delighted. She thanked the trainer and offered him her blessings.
The neighbors were very surprised by this. That disobedient, rebellious boy was gone, and in his place was a calm, peaceful, well-mannered boy.

His teacher welcomed the change too. Soon, however, a different problem emerged. Though the boy no longer openly rebelled, he stole classmates’ belongings, hid what he was doing, and lied. The teacher summoned his mother. Desperate, she went looking for the trainer, but he had left.
A neighbor suggested that she consult a wise, kindhearted man.
She took her son to him and explained. “Let him visit me for a week,” he said. “I’ll see what I can do.” She agreed.
She began bringing the boy to him.

After two meetings, the man spoke to her with concern. “What has happened to this child? He behaves like a frightened animal.” She explained that she had taken him to a bear trainer because he was so disobedient.

“An animal trainer?” he exclaimed. “You want to help a child develop a conscience, not frighten him into obedience. Beating, punishment, and confinement can produce fear, but fear is not an education.”
“Reach his heart,” he continued. “Be close to him. Hug him, listen to him, and let him know he is loved. When he feels safe with you, trust can begin to grow.”
“Neither the bear trainer nor I can take your place. He needs you, his parents.”

items.title: The Red Dress
items.moral: Moral: Loving others should not mean abandoning your own life. Leave room for your needs and hopes too.
body: The red dress was hanging in my mother's wardrobe. It seemed to shine next to the worn, faded clothes she had worn all her life.
When I came to my mother’s bedside, I could see that she was nearing the end of her life.
Seeing the red dress, I said to her:
“What a beautiful dress, Mom. I’ve never seen you wear it.”
“I never have,” she said softly. “Sit beside me, my dear. There’s something I want to tell you before I go.”
I sat down on the edge of the bed. My mother took a deep breath. “I don’t have much time left,” she said and continued:
“I thought I had always set you a good example. Now I’m afraid I taught you something very wrong.”
“What do you mean, Mom?”

“I believed a good woman should always put everyone else first. Their wishes mattered; mine could wait. I kept thinking my turn would come, but it never did. My whole life became a sacrifice for your father and all of you children.”
“But you did everything for us.”
“Yes, and I forgot to want anything for myself. Your father is sitting in the next room, upset and staring at the walls. When the doctor told him I was dying, he came in and said:
“‘You can’t die. What am I supposed to do without you?’

“I worked seven days a week, the first up and the last to bed. I ate the burned toast and the smallest portions. Every spare coin went on your clothes and books, even things you didn’t really need. I never bought myself anything lovely until last year, when I used the money saved for a washing-machine repair to buy that red dress. Your father was furious.
“‘Where do you think you’ll wear that? To the opera?’ he asked.
“And there it stayed. The only time I ever wore it was in the shop.

“I used to think that denying myself everything here would bring happiness in the next world. Now I believe Allah wants us to enjoy life here too. If I could get out of this bed, I would live differently.”
These were my mother’s last words to me:
“Promise me you won’t do what I did.”
I promised my mother and she breathed her last.

items.title: Meat for the Feast
items.moral: Moral: A celebration is complete only when others can share in it. In times of abundance, remember the neighbors who are going without.
body: I was in fifth grade. We were managing well enough then. My father, a builder, had joined a housing cooperative, and we hoped to move into our own home within six or seven months.

One morning we woke up to a terrible shaking. There had been an earthquake. Thankfully, nothing bad had happened to us or to those around us. No one in our building was hurt. But although our house and our lives were safe, this event brought another trouble to our family: as a result of the earthquake, construction work had stopped, and my father was unemployed.
No matter how hard we tried to save, the money my father earned from the repair jobs he found from time to time was not enough to support our household.
My father couldn't find work all winter. He would go with hope and return sad.
A few days before Ramadan, he came home beaming: someone had offered him work. “They told me to bring my papers,” he said, hurrying out again. “I need to get them there today.”
A few hours had passed when our neighbor came in with a panicked expression on his face.
“Don’t be afraid, but your father has had a minor accident,” he said.

At the hospital, we found him pale, his arms and legs bandaged. A driver had run a red light and hit him. As we gave thanks that he was alive, he tried to hide his tears. “Why did I survive?” he whispered. “Now I’ve made things even harder for you.”

After a while, my father came home. Our stove wasn’t burning, our house was cold. Several of our neighbors had called the municipality and asked for coal for us. “No way,” they said — we had to register in advance.
Eid al-Fitr came and went without sweets. At least the weather was warmer, and my father’s arm had healed, though his leg was still bandaged.

Then came Eid al-Adha. I thought to myself: “There are twelve apartments in our building, many of them will sacrifice. At least they will give us a share, and my mother will cook my favorite meat dishes.” As I watched from the window, the sacrificial animals were slaughtered, skinned, and bowls of meat were carried to the houses in the empty area opposite. Every time the door was opened, the delicious smell of meat being roasted in the houses spread to our house. But unfortunately, no one brought us a piece of meat.

Meanwhile, my grandmother called from the village to congratulate us on our holiday. She sensed that I was worried by the sound of my voice as she spoke. She asked insistently and anxiously: “Has your father gotten worse?”
“No,” I said slowly. “The neighbors didn’t give us sacrificial meat.”
In the summer months, we would go to the village to my grandmother. She had a cow and five or six chickens. Her cow gave good milk. When she milked it, my grandmother would sing songs to her.

On the third day of the holiday, there was a knock on our door early in the morning. It was my grandmother who came. We welcomed her with joy. She hugged us all, crying. “My lambs, my lambs, I brought you a lot of meat,” she said.

We filled the refrigerator with meat. My sister cut some up to cook, and the smell made my mouth water. Too hungry to wait for the table, I lifted a piece from the pan with a fork. Just as I was about to eat, I heard my father say:
“Mother, why did you slaughter your cow?”
My heart pounded. I dropped the fork and ran outside. The cow she sang to as she milked it, her precious source of income—had she given it up because I wanted meat?
When the table was ready, they coaxed me back. I tried to eat, but the food stuck in my throat and tears filled my eyes. “What’s wrong?” they asked.
“My tooth,” I said. “It hurts.”

items.title: An Eraser for Marriage
items.moral: Moral: Marriage is the art of forgiveness. For love and respect to continue, both parties must be able to "erase" each other's flaws.
body: A father wanted to share a lesson with his newly married son.
The father asked his newly married son for a sheet of paper, a pencil, and an eraser.
“Why?”
“Just bring them.”
The son found paper and a pencil, but no eraser.
“Then go and buy one.”
Puzzled, the son bought an eraser and sat down beside him.
“Write something.”
“What should I write?”
“Anything you like.”
The son wrote a sentence.
“Now erase it.”
He erased it.
“Write another sentence.”
“Father, please tell me what this is about.”
“Write one more.”
The son wrote again, and his father asked him to erase it.
After repeating this several times, the father asked:
“Is the paper still white?”
“Yes. But what does that mean?”
His father rested a hand on his shoulder.

“A marriage needs an eraser too, son. You will both make mistakes and do things the other dislikes. Each of you must be willing to erase some of those marks. Otherwise, the page you share will soon be covered with them.
“If you want love and respect, offer them to each other. And remember the eraser.”

items.title: What Women Have Endured
items.moral: Moral: There can be no peace or love where a woman is not valued. It is the duty of society to see her work and heart.
body: What have women endured in this world?
Even in fairy tales, they made her either a witch or a stepmother...
Stories burdened women with every accusation.
A woman was rarely allowed to be herself, though she gave life, nurtured it, and loved without conditions.
Woman...
They told her that her hair was long and her mind was short.
“Your hands are covered in flour. Stay in the kitchen. Don’t interfere.”
Woman, how much you have endured.
Few people knew your worth.
Few people could see your love, your heart, your goodness.
They called you wicked when you asked for your rights and virtuous when you kept silent.
Some mistook your love for a wish to control them.
Sometimes, those you raised to the heavens with your love preferred to stay there and forgot about you.
They did not ask how you were or whether you needed help.
They scarcely noticed whether you were there.
They forgot that you had a soul.
They forgot that you were human.
They wore you down, crushed your spirit, and ignored you.
Yet you wanted only to help, to care, and to make life better.
Your soul wandered in this world in need of love.
They talked about heaven and made you experience hell.
They looked into your eyes and denied the pain they saw. They would not hear the cry within you.
You loved being a mother, looking into your child’s eyes. In that child’s embrace, you found an affection you could trust.
